title: The Coming Risks to Russian Power
gist: A Moscow-based analyst argues Western assessments of Russia as a fading power are wrong for today's conditions — fragmentation, arms races, deglobalization and nationalism all play to Russian strengths — but that Russia's entire position is a leveraged bet on continued global disorder, and the pendulum's swing back toward stability would strip its military, resource and autocratic advantages of value.

themes.theme: Russia is not in terminal decline

insights.claim: Thirty-five years after the Soviet collapse, Russia remains a nuclear superpower and is still the benchmark threat around which NATO plans its forces, so the Western narrative of terminal Russian decline is at odds with reality.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Investors pricing a Russian capitulation scenario in Ukraine are betting against the author's base case of a durable stalemate and slow normalization.
insights.quote: This picture of Russia as feeble and fading may suit the biases of Putin’s many critics, but it is fundamentally at odds with reality: Moscow consistently punches above its weight in global affairs.
insights.locator: This picture of Russia as feeble and fading

insights.claim: An unprecedented wall of Western sanctions has failed to trigger the economic collapse its architects predicted or to erode Russian political and social stability.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Supports fading headlines about each new sanctions package as a driver of Russian behavior; incremental sanctions have low marginal impact on the war's duration.
insights.quote: An unprecedented wall of Western sanctions has failed to trigger the economic collapse its architects predicted
insights.locator: An unprecedented wall of Western sanctions

insights.claim: Russia's isolation campaign has faltered because the Kremlin has built out BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, extending its influence over the post-Western order now taking shape.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Non-Western institutional plumbing (payments, commodity settlement, development finance) is a growth area; Western sanctions leakage runs through it.
insights.locator: The effort to isolate Moscow has faltered

insights.claim: Four and a half years of fighting have transformed Russia's armed forces from the flawed force exposed in February 2022 into one of the world's strongest militaries with unique experience in next-generation ground warfare — an edge over almost any other force, the United States included.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: A structural argument for sustained European defense spending and for the premium on combat-proven drone and electronic-warfare capability.
insights.quote: has unique experience in next-generation ground warfare—an edge over almost any other fighting force, the United States included

insights.claim: Ukraine's battlefield adaptations may not survive the end of the fighting because they depend on Western support, whereas Russia's accumulated combat experience is institutional and persists.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: A postwar Ukraine defense-industrial base is not a given; its drone-sector durability depends on continued Western procurement commitments.
insights.locator: Ukraine, too, has adapted its forces

insights.claim: Russia's outsized influence is conditional on today's international conditions — volatility, active conflicts and arms races, economic decoupling, the retreat of globalization, rising nationalism and populism, the discounting of soft power, and fissures in the Western alliance all work to Moscow's advantage.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Gives a testable list of regime indicators: as any of these reverse, Russian leverage and therefore Russian risk premia should fall.
insights.locator: This bullish assessment comes with a caveat

insights.claim: A divided, resource-scarce world magnifies Russia's commodity leverage precisely because supply, not price, has become the priority for buyers across oil, gas, coal, wheat, fertilizers, uranium, critical metals and diamonds.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Security-of-supply buying supports structurally wider spreads for politically safe barrels and tonnes; uranium and fertilizer are the least substitutable Russian exposures.
insights.quote: It regularly plays the role of dealmaker, especially now that supply, not price, is the priority.

insights.claim: China's continued reliance on Russian fossil fuels offsets the asymmetry in the Moscow-Beijing relationship even as Europe weans itself off those supplies, so Russia is less of a Chinese vassal than Western analysts assume.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Chinese refiners' dependence on discounted Russian crude is a standing constraint on how far Beijing will cooperate with Western energy sanctions.
insights.locator: Europe, for instance, may be weaning itself off

insights.claim: The vulnerability of Middle Eastern supply routes during the Iran war has further strengthened Russia's hand as a commodity supplier and dealmaker.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Hormuz-type disruptions transfer rent directly to Russia — a hedge relationship worth tracking between Gulf risk and Russian export revenue.
insights.locator: The vulnerability of Middle Eastern supply routes

insights.claim: In a polarized era, Russia's centralized, personalized decision-making is a comparative advantage over liberal democracies, because Putin faces little opposition, few establishment divisions and scant media pushback and can plan long-term in ways Western election cycles rule out.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Reframes autocratic governance as a strategic-planning asset in a fragmented world — relevant to any thesis that Western policy incoherence is a persistent discount factor.

insights.claim: Today's turmoil will end and global disorder will subside as the international system consolidates anew, at which point Russia's time-tested foreign policy and rigid institutions will stop serving it well.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: The core asymmetric risk to Russian assets and influence is not sanctions but normalization elsewhere in the world.
insights.quote: When this change happens—and it will—Russia may find that its time-tested foreign policy and its once reliable but rigid institutions no longer serve it well.

insights.claim: Specific triggers for the reversal include Trump leaving the White House with a successor who restores transatlantic support, multilateralism and open trade, a planetary shock such as accelerating climate change or an out-of-control AI system, or a major defeat for Trump's supporters in the coming U.S. midterm elections.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Gives dated catalysts — the U.S. midterms are the nearest — for a regime shift that would compress Russian geopolitical leverage.
insights.quote: The reversal of the pendulum could begin as early as the coming midterm elections in the United States

insights.claim: In a re-globalized world Russia would lack the offsets others have: its demographic decline forecloses a China- or India-sized domestic market, falling fossil fuel demand kills the export-more-hydrocarbons route, and attracting large-scale FDI requires trust, transparency and a stable legal framework Russia does not offer.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Three independent structural headwinds mean any long-run bull case on Russian assets requires a political regime change, not just a peace deal.
insights.locator: In such a world, some of the foreign policy assets

insights.claim: Russia's twentieth-century Soviet state-centered innovation model cannot produce competitiveness in AI and robotics, clean energy, quantum computing and gene editing, because two decades of tightening state control over the private sector have suffocated the entrepreneurial energy those fields require.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Russia should be assumed a permanent technology importer, deepening its dependence on China for anything beyond commodities and weapons.
insights.locator: Finally, without a strong civilian high-tech ecosystem

insights.claim: Russia's longest-in-the-world Arctic coastline gives it a claim on High North resources and new warming-opened shipping routes, but monetizing the East Asia-to-Europe transit corridor requires stable long-term partnerships with the EU as well as China — relationships that are hard to imagine now.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Arctic transit is a real long-dated option on Russia-EU normalization, not a near-term trade.
insights.locator: The country’s geography offers some advantage

insights.claim: Russia's 'besieged fortress' model treats the international environment as a challenge rather than an opportunity, minimizing immediate external risk while preventing full use of its geography, resources and human capital.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: A framework for reading Kremlin policy: expect risk-minimizing, growth-sacrificing choices to persist even after a Ukraine settlement.
insights.quote: Perpetual confrontation with the United States and Europe does not serve Russia’s long-term development.

insights.claim: Restoring ties with the European Union matters more to Russia's long-run development than any other relationship, because EU member states were once Moscow's main economic partners and its chief source of new technology and modern business practices — and repair could begin once the Ukraine conflict ends.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: A Ukraine ceasefire would open a slow, multi-year Russia-EU commercial normalization trade rather than an immediate one.
insights.locator: Restoring ties with the EU matters most of all

insights.claim: A 'might makes right' world offers Moscow real short-run opportunities but is a dangerous long-run game, because the balance of power is shifting fast and new actors are rising — making a strong international legal system one of the few safeguards against revisionists targeting Russia itself.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: A Russian insider arguing for norms on self-interested grounds signals awareness that Russia becomes a target, not just a beneficiary, of multipolar predation.
insights.locator: It is also in Russia’s own interest to do its part

insights.claim: Russia's preference for stability over change is rooted in the trauma of the 1990s, when change came as catastrophe, but that preference can harden into a refusal to adapt — the calcification that has pushed great powers to the sidelines before.
insights.speaker: Andrey Kortunov
insights.so_what: Explains why Kremlin policy will likely under-adapt to a changing world: the political cost of reform is remembered as existential.
insights.quote: that preference can also harden into a refusal to adapt—a calcification that has pushed great powers to the sidelines before
insights.locator: Russia is, to the dismay of its critics, holding strong
